newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian snapshot shows more claim native descent.
newsitem.headline: Australian snapshot shows more claim native descent.

text.p: More Australians are claiming Aboriginal heritage as old stigmas fade, according to a snapshot of the nation released on Tuesday.

As populist politician Pauline Hanson tours the country fighting immigration and Aboriginal policies, the official Bureau of Statistics released details of the last national census, in 1996, which paints a picture of an increasingly diverse nation.

The bureau said Australians were increasingly willing to claim indigenous heritage -- with a 33 percent jump in native numbers since the previous census in 1991 due more to the way people saw themselves than an increased indigenous birth rate.
"This increase is partly explained by people's increased willingness to declare their indigenous origin," the bureau said in its overview of its findings on the 1996 census.
An indigenous affairs expert with the bureau said native affairs had taken a higher profile in recent years.

"I think it's just general increase in the level of interest throughout the country in indigenous issues over the past few years that has undoubtedly had some effect," Tony Barnes told Reuters from Darwin, capital of the outback Northern Territory.
Aborigines and Torres Strait islanders now account for 2.0 percent, or 352,970 people, of the national population, up from 1.6 percent, or 265,458 in 1991.
At the same time, the proportion of Australians born on this vast island continent fell to 73.9 percent, or 13.2 million, from 75.5 percent, or 12.7 million, over the five years.
The proportion of Asian-born Australians -- an issue that has spurred Hanson's popularity -- increased to 4.8 percent, or 856,144, from 4.1 percent, or 687,850, in 1991.
The 24.5 percent increase in Asian-born Australians outstripped the total population growth of 6.2 percent, to 17.9 million from 16.9 million.
Hanson sparked a divisive national row last year when she warned Australia was in danger of being swamped by Asians, and criticised Australia's Aboriginal policies.

She was dumped from Prime Minister John Howard's Liberal Party ahead of the March 1996 election for comments seen as racist, but has since launched her own One Nation Party and draws enough opinion poll support to make her a serious force in domestic politics.
The census -- a nationwide poll of every household in the country on one night in August last year -- also found Australians' average age is increasing.
The median age now is 34 compared with 32 in 1991, reinforcing government efforts to boost workers' retirement savings so they can fund their own retirement instead of relying on government pensions.
The census also showed that women outnumber men in Australia -- nationally Australia's population is now 50.5 percent female and 49.5 percent male.
Australia conducts a census every five years.
